t: the Great Court in Jerusalem. Which has seventy-one judges and sits in the Chamber of Hewn Stone in the Temple (Hilchot Sanhedrin 1:3).
and about them the Torah gave assurance. The Torah said that one should trust and rely on their ruling (compare Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 11:1).
he is obligated to rely on them in the practice of religion and lean on them. To act as they rule and accept their authority upon himself.

and one is not flogged for this prohibition because it was given as a warning of death by the court, etc.. Since this prohibition essentially refers to the law of the rebellious elder who is liable to death (as explained below 3:4 ff.), it turns out that this prohibition does not come to warn of flogging. Therefore even a person who is not a rebellious elder, if he transgresses the ruling of the Sages, is not liable to flogging (for this rule see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).
who rebelled. Revolted and refused.
as it says: and the man who acts presumptuously. And later in the verse it says: "and that man shall die," and an unspecified death in the Torah is by strangulation (Hilchot Sanhedrin 14:1).
matters that they learned by oral tradition, which are the Oral Torah. Interpretations and laws that were transmitted by oral tradition from Moses our teacher.
by one of the principles by which the Torah is expounded. By one of the accepted methods of expounding Scripture.
these are the decrees. Laws that the prophets and Sages established as a fence around the laws of the Torah, to ensure that they are not transgressed.
and the enactments. Laws made to regulate matters between one person and another or for the betterment of the world as the hour requires.

and the customs. Things that the people, or individual Sages, adopted on their own, and the Great Court agreed to them and instructed all the people to follow them (for details of these concepts see Maimonides' introduction to the Commentary on the Mishnah).
matters of Kabbalah. That were transmitted from Moses our teacher.
and matters learned by logical inference. Matters that the Sages learned on their own using one of the principles by which the Torah is expounded.
he asks the court in his city. For in every city in the Land of Israel there is a commandment to establish a court (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 1:1-2).

and they ask the court on the Temple Mount... they come to the court at the entrance of the Temple courtyard, etc.. For in addition to the Great Court in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, there are two more courts of twenty-three judges on the Temple Mount, one sitting at the entrance to the Temple Mount and one at the entrance to the courtyard (ibid. 1:3).
they judge it at their time. They rule on it immediately, and do not refer to another tribunal.
when there is no Sanhedrin. After the Great Court ceased to exist.

or before the matter had reached them. That they disagreed while the Great Court existed, but this law had not yet been brought for its decision, and meanwhile one must know what to do (Lechem Mishneh).
whether at one time or one after the other. Whether the two sages lived in the same period or in different periods.
in a matter of Torah law. When the doubt concerns a law from the Torah.
and in a matter of rabbinic law. A law from the Sages.

he cannot, unless he is greater than the earlier ones in wisdom and in number. This applies specifically to annulling decrees and enactments, but a law that was derived by one of the principles of exposition, a court may annul the words of earlier ones even though it is not greater than they in wisdom and number (Radbaz, Kesef Mishneh and others).

in wisdom. That the head of the present court is wiser than the previous one (Commentary on the Mishnah, Eduyot 1:5). Some wrote that it is also necessary that the total wisdom of the whole court together exceeds the wisdom of the previous court (Responsa of the Radbaz 5:117).

to make a fence. Decrees whose purpose is to distance a person from transgression (see an example below 2:9), as distinct from the enactments and customs of the Sages for regulating matters between people or for the betterment of the world and the like (based on Maimonides' introduction to the Commentary on the Mishnah; and see Merkevet HaMishneh, who explained Maimonides' words here differently).
temporarily. On a temporary basis.
every court has. Any court is permitted.
they flog not according to law and punish not according to law. See Hilchot Sanhedrin 24:4-5.

and likewise if they saw, temporarily, to nullify a positive commandment or to transgress a negative commandment... they do as the hour requires. Similarly is the law for a prophet who says to transgress the words of the Torah temporarily, as Elijah did on Mount Carmel (see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 9:3).

just as a physician cuts off the hand or foot of one so that the whole person may live, etc.. For all the commandments are considered as one body, and therefore at times it is necessary to uproot one so that the religion as a whole will be maintained (see Radbaz).
as the early Sages said. Regarding the permission to desecrate Shabbat to save a life (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 85b).
they must deliberate on the matter. To examine it carefully with settled mind.
and after they decreed it, the people were doubtful about it. That its observance was lax among them.

they decreed and imagined that it spread throughout Israel... he has permission to annul it. This applies specifically in a case where they imagined that it spread throughout Israel; but if the decree truly spread throughout Israel, even if after much time they checked and found that it no longer spreads throughout Israel, it cannot be annulled (the conclusion of the Kesef Mishneh and the opinion of many commentators). It is possible to explain that even if the enactment initially spread throughout Israel, if now most of Israel are not careful about it, the later court may annul it (the initial understanding of the Kesef Mishneh, and so explained by Yad Peshutah).
and to establish the matter forever as from the Torah. But to establish something for generations as rabbinic law is permitted.

whether the Written Torah or the Oral Torah. The prohibition of adding to and subtracting from the words of the Torah refers both to matters explicit in the Written Torah and to matters of the Torah that were stated in the tradition of the Oral Torah.
and by oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in interpreting the verses.

whether the flesh of an ox or the flesh of a sheep, etc.. See Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 9:4 [Note: the text here follows the responsum of R. Yehoshua HaNagid (no. 45), who wrote that this is the text in a book corrected from Maimonides' own copy. In the other manuscripts and printings the text is: "whether the flesh of an animal or the flesh of a wild beast." And likewise in the next paragraph: "if a court should come and permit the flesh of a sheep in milk," in place of the words "flesh of a sheep," the manuscripts and printings read: "flesh of a wild beast." It appears that the text before us is a correction Maimonides made in his book that fits his position in Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot there, that the flesh of a wild beast in milk is not forbidden by the Torah (see R. Y. Shilat in Rambam Meduyak, who discussed this at length).]
a ruin. A mishap.

and another will come and say that the flesh of an animal is also permitted except for goat. For the verse explicitly mentions only "a kid," and elsewhere in the Torah it is clear that a kid is of the goat species (Genesis 27:16, 38:20; based on Babylonian Talmud, Chullin 113a).

one who does not believe in the Oral Torah. Who denies the interpretation of the Torah as received in tradition, and relies only on the Written Torah as he himself interprets it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 11:3, and see Hilchot Teshuvah 3:8).
is among the heretics. People who deny the fundamental principles of faith (see Hilchot Teshuvah 3:6-8).
and his death is in the hand of any person. See Hilchot Rotzeach 4:10.

they lower him but do not raise him. They push him down by force into a pit or other deadly danger in order to kill him, and if he fell into a pit by himself, they prevent him from getting out, for example by removing the ladder and the like.
like the other heretics and epicureans, etc.. See also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:1, Hilchot Edut 11:10.
and the informers. People who hand over their fellows or their property to gentiles or violent people (Hilchot Teshuvah 3:12, and see also Hilchot Chovel U'Mazik 8:9-10).

and the apostates. Those who transgress deliberately and in rebellion against God's commandments, even those who transgress a single transgression to spite (Hilchot Teshuvah 3:9, Hilchot Rotzeach 4:10).
and he denied the Oral Torah at first. That he began to deny it on his own, and was not raised to it.
and likewise all who err after him. Those who followed him and erred in the same matter.
and they raised them on it. They raised and educated them on views of heresy.

they are like an infant who was captured among the gentiles... who is under duress. And therefore he is not to be killed. However, with regard to the obligation of an offering, he is judged as having sinned unintentionally and is liable for a sin offering for his transgressions (Hilchot Shegagot 2:6).

until they return to the strength of the Torah. Until they discover their error and return to firm faith in the Torah (compare the expression "strong" said of Abraham our forefather in Hilchot Avodah Zarah 1:3).
who has a tradition. Who received legal traditions from his teachers.

and he confesses and has a share in the World to Come. As is the way of all those put to death by the court, who confess before their execution so that they will have a share in the World to Come (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 13:1), and unlike heretics and epicureans, who have no share in the World to Come (Hilchot Teshuvah 3:6).
a sage who has reached the level of ruling. Who is expert in the whole Torah and is fit to be ordained (Hilchot Sanhedrin 4:8, and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 11:2).
ordained in the Sanhedrin. Ordained by the court (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:1).
in a matter for which one is liable for karet for deliberate transgression and a sin offering for unintentional transgression. As explained below 4:2.
or concerning tefillin. See below 4:3.
and they sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone. Which is their place of sitting (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:17).

one from whom only a hidden matter is hidden. Only someone to whom difficult and complex laws are unknown is fit to become a rebellious elder, not a student who has not reached the level of ruling and does not know even simple and well-known matters.
a distinguished sage of the court. Who is fit to rule on the whole Torah and was ordained by the court (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 4:8).
he found them outside their place. The sages of the Great Court were outside the Chamber of Hewn Stone.
at the time a matter is hidden. When a doubt arises about some law.
and they come to the court at the entrance of the Temple Mount, etc.. See above 1:4.
and he taught and instructed as he was accustomed. He studied himself and taught others according to the halachic opinion he held, but did not rule that one should act that way in practice.

and he does not require a warning. Unlike other people liable to death by the court, who are not executed unless they were warned before the act (Hilchot Sanhedrin 12:1-2), a rebellious elder does not need a warning, since he already knows that what he is doing is forbidden (Radbaz, and see Rulings and Opinions).
and they keep him until the festival. They delay his execution until the nearest of the three pilgrimage festivals arrives, when there is a multitude of people in Jerusalem.
and they strangle him. For the death of a rebellious elder is by strangulation (above 1:2, Hilchot Sanhedrin 15:13).
by implication that it requires a proclamation. That his execution must be announced publicly.
elder. Sage.
in a matter for which one is liable for karet for deliberate transgression and a sin offering for unintentional transgression. As will be explained later in this chapter.
by tradition. That he received by tradition.

such as one who permitted chametz on the fourteenth at the sixth hour, etc.. By Torah law chametz is forbidden on the eve of Pesach (the fourteenth of Nisan) from the seventh hour of the day, and the Sages forbade eating and benefiting from it already from the beginning of the sixth hour in order to distance people from a Torah prohibition, and they further decreed not to eat chametz from the fifth hour out of concern that one might confuse the fifth and sixth hours, but did not then forbid benefiting from the chametz (Hilchot Chametz U'Matzah 1:8-10). A rebellious elder who permits it in the sixth hour or who forbids benefit in the fifth hour disputes the Sages in their decree regarding chametz, which is a prohibition for which one is basically liable to karet for deliberate transgression and a sin offering for unintentional transgression (Meiri, Sanhedrin 88a, Radbaz; and see Kesef Mishneh, who explained differently).
and according to the one who says that it is his, he took, etc.. And it turns out that his betrothal is a valid betrothal, and the woman is considered a married woman.
they are injuring him and are liable to pay. For the court's agents who flog a person unlawfully are judged as injuring their fellow and are liable for payments.

in valuations or in dedications. For example, they disagreed about a particular case in which a person obligated himself to give a person's valuation to the Temple, or dedicated some item for the needs of the Temple or the priests.
he is liable. A rebellious elder who disputes in this matter is liable to death.

in the breaking of the heifer's neck, etc.. When a slain person is found near a certain city and it is not known who killed him, its inhabitants must bring a heifer and break its neck in a stream, and it is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Rotzeach 10:6).
and one who betroths a woman with it, she is not betrothed. For one who betroths with something that is forbidden for benefit, the woman is not betrothed (Hilchot Ishut 5:1).

and likewise if they disagreed about orlah. For example, they disagreed about a certain plant whether it is subject to orlah or not (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 11:2). And orlah is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 10:9).
in leket, shikchah and peah. Gifts from the produce that a landowner must give to the poor.
such as skin blemishes, etc.. That they disagreed about certain leprous blemishes whether they are pure or impure.

and according to the one who says impure, if he entered or ate... and if unintentionally he brings a sin offering. For an impure person who entered the Temple unintentionally or ate sacred food unintentionally brings an offering of variable value, which is a type of sin offering (see Hilchot Shegagot 1:1-4, Yad Peshutah).

and likewise if they disagreed about the purification of a leper, whether this one has purification or has none. For example, a leper who has no thumb, big toe, or right ear (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 88a, and see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 5:1).
in giving the sotah to drink. A woman whose husband warned her and who secluded herself is forbidden to her husband until she is tested by the bitter waters that cause a curse (Hilchot Sotah 1:1-2).

according to the one who says she needs it, if the husband died before she drank, she is forbidden to her yavam. For a sotah whose husband died before she drank does not undergo yibbum (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 6:19). And since there is no commandment of yibbum here, the yavam has relations with his brother's wife in a forbidden way, and is liable for karet if deliberate and a sin offering if unintentional (Rabbi Akiva Eger there, Arukh LaNer, Yevamot 11b and others).

whether she is forbidden relations or not. Whether she is forbidden to this man by a prohibition of forbidden relations (for example, because she is his relative), such that if he had relations with her deliberately he is liable to karet, and if unintentionally, to a sin offering.

whether this blood appearance is impure or is not impure. For if the woman saw blood that renders her impure, she becomes a niddah and one who has relations with her is liable to karet or a sin offering (for the details of blood that renders impure see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah chapter 5).

whether this one is impure from childbirth or is not impure from childbirth. For a woman who gave birth is impure like a niddah, specifically when she gave birth to or miscarried something that makes her impure (as explained there, chapter 10).

whether this one is a zavah or is not a zavah. For if she saw blood on certain days she becomes a zavah (see ibid. 6:1-6), and one who has relations with her is liable like one who has relations with a niddah.
whether this fat is forbidden or permitted. For one who eats forbidden fat is liable to karet or a sin offering (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot chapter 7 for which fats are forbidden).

whether they intercalate until Purim or throughout Adar. They disagreed on the question whether it can be decided that the year is a leap year and an additional month of Adar added to it only until Purim arrives, or whether this can be done until the end of the month of Adar (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 4:13-14).

for this leads to eating chametz on Pesach. For the decision about intercalating the year affects the time at which the festival of Pesach falls, and it turns out that the dispute about it affects the time of the prohibition of eating chametz, which is something for which one is liable to karet for deliberate transgression and a sin offering for unintentional transgression.
or in the number of judges who judge monetary cases. They disagreed about how many judges may judge monetary cases (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 2:10).
according to the words of one, etc.. This explains why this dispute leads to a sin offering or karet.
and if he betroths a woman with it, she is not betrothed. For one who betroths with something that is not his, the woman is not betrothed (Hilchot Ishut 5:7).
to add a fifth totefet to the tefillin. An additional compartment to the four compartments in the head tefillin.

for an outer compartment that does not see the air is invalid. The outermost compartment on the right or left must be exposed to the air, and if one adds another compartment next to it and blocks it, the tefillin are invalid.
by tradition. A halachic tradition.

and this one says second-degree impurity. And at this degree of impurity one does not become liable to karet or a sin offering for entering the Temple (see Kesef Mishneh, and see Keter HaMelech, who explained differently).

he is stoned, as it says... his blood is upon him. And the Sages learned that wherever this expression is written in the Torah it means stoning (Sifra, Kedoshim, chapter 9, halachah 14, and see also Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 66b).
the tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and whose sex is unclear. [Note: Maimonides vocalizes this word in the Commentary on the Mishnah as tumtom.]
and the androginos. One who has both male and female organs.

provided that they are adults who have reached the category of those subject to punishments. For only when they are defined as adults are they liable to punishments (for the criteria of reaching adulthood see Hilchot Ishut chapter 2).
by one of the special names. One of the seven names that are not erased (see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:2).
by an epithet. One of the epithets of the Name, such as "Merciful" and "Gracious" (ibid. 6:5).

and is flogged as one is flogged for cursing any fit Israelite. For one who curses an Israelite who is not his father or mother is liable to flogging, even if he cursed him with an epithet (Hilchot Sanhedrin 26:3; and specifically one who curses a fit person, but one who curses a wicked person is exempt - see Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 85a and Or Sameach there, and see below 12).
we heard the punishment explicitly. See above 1.
but the warning is included in: You shall not curse a deaf person, etc.. From this verse it is learned that it is forbidden to curse any Israelite, not only a deaf person (Hilchot Sanhedrin 26:1).
his death is by strangulation, as it says... he shall surely die. And an unspecified "death" mentioned in the Torah is by strangulation (Hilchot Sanhedrin 14:1).
a wound. A blow that draws blood.

he is like one who strikes any other Israelite. He is not liable to death but transgresses a negative commandment (Hilchot Chovel 5:1), and must pay the five payments that one who injures his fellow pays (ibid. 4:7).

even a drop of blood came out internally in the ear and he became deaf. Even though it is not seen at all that a wound was made, it suffices that only a single drop of blood came out internally and caused him to become deaf for the blow to be considered a wound for which one is liable to death.
and cut for him flesh or a limb. For his healing.
even though he is exempt, initially he should not do so. Lest he wound them more than necessary for their healing (Kesef Mishneh).
a thorn. A thorn.
we heard the punishment. See above 5.
since he is warned not to strike an Israelite. Hilchot Chovel 5:1, Hilchot Sanhedrin 16:12.
a shetuki. A person whose father is not known with certainty (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:12).
is liable for his mother. If he cursed or struck her.

but his son from a maidservant or a gentile woman is not liable for his father or his mother. For he is not considered his son but follows the mother and has the status of a slave or gentile, and after he is freed or converts he is considered a newborn minor and is not related to his parents.

a convert whose conception was not in holiness, although he was born in holiness, is not liable for striking his father or cursing him. For since his mother was a gentile when she conceived, although she converted before the birth, so that her son is an Israelite and does not require conversion, nevertheless he is not liable for his father because he is not related to him.

so that they not say they came from a greater holiness to a lesser holiness. Although gentiles are not commanded to honor parents, since they behave this way by their own norms, they forbade a convert to disgrace his father, so that it should not appear that conversion permits prohibitions (Pri Megadim, Igeret 3, par. 20, cited by Rabbi Akiva Eger; for another example see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:12).

but a slave has no lineage, etc.. A slave is not related to his father at all and does not treat him with honor even while he is a slave, and therefore even after he is freed he has no obligation of honor toward him at all.
and if he cursed or injured them he is exempt. For one is liable only for a fit person (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 85a, and see above 2).

in what case is this said? In his son, etc.. The Sages learned that the liability of one who curses applies only to a person who is to live and survive, and not to one whose sentence to death has been completed, and from the curser they learned that the same applies to the striker (see Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 85a). However, since one who curses his parents is liable even after their death (above 1), it turns out that even after their sentence of death is complete he is liable for cursing them, and therefore by the same reasoning he is also liable for striking them (Binyan Shlomo, Sanhedrin 85b, and see another explanation in Rashi there).
and if he shamed him he is liable for the fine of one who shames. For even when his sentence of death has been completed, he is liable for payment for shame, like anyone who shames his fellow.
and he was an attendant before the judges. His job is to flog those liable to flogging (Hilchot Sanhedrin 16:8).
except for an enticer. For if his father enticed to idolatry, the son may be an agent of the court even to strike him or curse him.
one who became obligated to take an oath to his son. That his son claimed money from him in court, and the judges obligated him to take an oath on his claim.

he may not administer to him the oath with the curse, for this leads to the cursing of his father. One obligated to take an oath in court can take an ordinary oath, or an oath with a curse, which is an oath that includes a curse toward the one swearing in the event that he is lying (see Hilchot Shevuot 11:8). One who sues his father in court and obligates him to take an oath administers an oath that has no curse, so that he not come to cursing his father if it becomes clear that he lied.
and we have already explained. Hilchot Rotzeach 1:3.
none of the brothers of one who was killed becomes the blood avenger. Even though there is a commandment upon him to be the blood avenger (ibid. 5:2), he is forbidden to kill his father.
in words. In speech.
belittles. Treats with contempt.

and behold it says: The eye that mocks a father, etc.. From this verse one can learn that even a wink alone can mock a father and shame him and harm discipline toward the mother (see the commentators there).
a rebellious beating. Lashes by rabbinic law.
and to punish as they see fit. See also Hilchot Sanhedrin 26:5.
one who curses his father or mother is stoned. Above 5:1.
and the blasphemer. One who curses God.
by stoning. Hilchot Avodah Zarah 2:6.

He put the father before the mother in honor, and put the mother before the father in fear. In the commandment to honor parents, the father is mentioned first (Exodus 20:12, Deuteronomy 5:16). In contrast, in the commandment to fear them, the mother is mentioned first (Leviticus 19:3).
he does not stand in his place. His fixed place.
and does not contradict his words. He does not say things against his father's words.
and does not decide his words. He does not decide in an argument that another person is having with his father.
and he does not call him by his name. His first name.

if the name of his father or of his teacher was like the names of others, he changes their name. That he is forbidden to call others by their name if it is the same as the name of his father or his teacher (for one is obligated to honor his teacher, see Hilchot Talmud Torah chapter 5), but calls them by a different epithet (see also ibid. 5:5).
Mari. My lor
by a name that is unusual. A rare and distinctive name, in which case using it shows contempt toward his father.
from the father's property. From the father's possessions.
and brings out and brings in. If they are old and need a hand to lean on (Rabbenu Chananel ben Shmuel, Kiddushin 31b).
and serves him in the other matters in which attendants serve a master. See Hilchot Talmud Torah 5:8.
and stands before him as he stands before his teacher. See ibid. 5:7.
at the time of his business dealings and the doing of his affairs. When he is engaged in the needs of his father's business and affairs.
one who is sent on his father's word to a place. Goes on his father's errand to a certain place.
and a woman is not able to do so, for she is under another's authority. For she is at her husband's disposal and occupied with her household, and cannot always engage in honoring her parents.
they are both equal. A man and a woman are equal regarding honoring their parents.
the decree of Scripture. The Torah's command.
precious garments. Fine and respectable clothes.
to be doubtful. To vacillate.
for he transgresses: and before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block. For it may cause the son to strike him back and thereby transgress a prohibition.

even though he is exempt for striking him and cursing him until he repents. For his father is a transgressor, having had relations with a forbidden relation and fathered a mamzer, and as long as he has not repented his son is exempt for striking him and cursing him (above 5:12).
but let him say to him: Father, it is written in the Torah thus and so. Similarly one should behave toward one's teacher (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 5:9).
of their words. The words of the Sages.
and there is a commandment to do. There is another commandment upon him to do at that time, for example one that cannot be postponed until afterward (Kesef Mishneh).
because he and his mother are obligated in the honor of his father. See Hilchot Ishut 15:20.
mentioned in the Torah. Deuteronomy 21:18-21.
eating that leads to bloodshed. This eating that ultimately leads to his being sentenced to death, with his blood on his own head (see Sefer HaMitzvot, negative commandment 195).
by oral tradition. The Sages' tradition in interpreting the verses.
matters. Conditions.
by tradition. A halachic tradition.
until he steals. Money.
and buys cheap meat and cheap wine. For when he buys cheap he may continue his actions, unlike expensive meat and wine, where it is hard for him to obtain enough money to buy them.
as thieves eat. For they eat in haste so as not to be caught, and have no time to cook it through.
and drinks the wine diluted and not diluted, as gluttons drink. As gluttons do, who mix only a little water into their wine.
the weight of fifty dinars. About 240 grams.

in one mouthful. That he put this entire amount of meat into his mouth at once and chews (see Tosefta Sanhedrin 11:6, Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 8:1), and some explain that it means he eats quickly without pause in the manner of gluttony (Radbaz).
half a log. About 150 cc.
by rabbinic law. From the words of the Sages.

this excludes one who transgressed a Torah law with it or ate it as part of a commandment. With regard to eating as part of a commandment, they expound: "he does not listen to our voice" - this excludes one who listens to the voice of his Father in heaven (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 8:2).
or who ate second tithe in Jerusalem. That he stole money of second tithe from his father and bought meat and wine with it in Jerusalem and ate there as commanded (Rashi, Sanhedrin 70b).
at a mourners' meal of consolation, which is a commandment by rabbinic law. See Hilchot Evel 14:1.
by chance. Accidentally.
and likewise if he ate salted meat on the third day after its salting. For from the third day onward it no longer has the actual taste of meat (compare Hilchot Ta'aniyot 5:7).
wine from its vat. Must, squeezed grape juice whose fermentation has not yet finished.
at thirteen years and one day, having grown two hairs. In the pubic area, whereupon he is defined as a man (Hilchot Ishut 2:10).
until the hair surrounds the entire organ. The male organ.

because it is possible that his wife will conceive and her pregnancy will be recognizable in three months, etc.. For after three months from when he grew two hairs and was considered an adult, he could be fit to be regarded as the father of a fetus in his wife's womb, and therefore he is no longer judged as a stubborn and rebellious son (even if he is not married).
so you have learned that if the hair surrounded the entire organ before he completed three months, he is exempt. For after this time he is in any case exempt since he is fit to be called a father.
to a court of three. That judges the cases of those liable to flogging (Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:4).
and he ate them in the eating described after the warning. That he ate and drank gluttonously under all the conditions stated above (halachot 2-4), after he was warned about it before two witnesses.

and they flog him like other people liable to flogging, as it says: and they shall chastise him and he does not listen to them. Although there is no specific prohibition here for which one is liable to flogging (for the warning of the stubborn and rebellious son based on "you shall not eat over the blood" is a general prohibition for which one is not flogged, as explained in Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:3), the flogging here is a special decree of Scripture (see Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 71b and Yad Ramah there 63a).
to a court of twenty-three. That judges capital cases (Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:2).
and he is not stoned unless the first three are there. That in the court that judges him to death, the three judges who judged him to flogging must be present.
if his father wished, etc.. To treat him with the law of a stubborn and rebellious son.
and they took hold of him, not the handless. Who cannot grasp.
and they brought him out, not the lame. For the lame cannot walk.
this son of ours, not the blind. For the blind cannot see and say "this."
he does not listen to our voice, not the deaf. For the deaf do not hear whether he accepted their words or not.
tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and whose sex is unclear.
and androginos. One who has both male and female organs.
a tumtum who was torn open. The membrane that covered his sexual organs was torn.
until he is a son from the time of his formation. Until it is clear that he is a son from the time he was born.
like all those executed by the court, whose money goes to their heirs. Hilchot Evel 1:9.
